title: The Changing Role of AI Agents in Science Must be Recognized
content: Current editorial guidelines from organizations such as the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE) treat generative artificial intelligence (AI) primarily as an administrative assistant or text manipulator, relegating its contributions to footnotes or acknowledgments. This policy framework misinterprets the operational reality of modern biomedical research, where advanced language models function as active intellectual partners capable of logical stress-testing, data synthesis, and hypothesis generation. Conflating operational cognitive contribution with legal and ethical accountability creates unnecessary opacity in scholarly publishing. To resolve this tension, this paper examines four structural credit frameworks—ranging from the institutional status quo to dual-track independent lists and expanded contributor taxonomies. We propose that medical publishing must evolve beyond obsolete binary definitions, establishing transparent attribution models that separate human regulatory liability from the recognition of machine-assisted scientific co-creation.
